patients.summary: 51-year-old teacher with type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity and chronic constipation who joined in 2020. Gallstones failed ursodiol dissolution, plantar fasciitis and overactive bladder settled with conservative care, rectal prolapse was repaired by rectopexy in 2024, and obstructive jaundice from a bile duct stone in December 2025 led to ERCP and cholecystectomy.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
New patient, 45F, transferring from a prior internal medicine office. Here to establish.

Problems she brings:
1. T2DM, dx around 2016 by prior PCP. Metformin 1000 BID since then, tolerating. Doesn't check sugars at home. Last A1c she remembers was "under 7." No known eye/kidney/nerve issues. Eye exam overdue.
2. Hypothyroid since ~2009, levothyroxine 100 mcg, same dose for years. Takes it first thing.
3. Weight. Has been in the low 180s for about 10 yrs. Tries to cut carbs, on and off.
4. Constipation for as long as she can remember, goes every 2-3 days, strains. Manages with prunes, water, salad. No blood, no weight loss.
Also takes a multivitamin and OTC ibuprofen 1-2 tabs now and then for aches after a long day standing.

PSH: none. No abdominal or pelvic surgery.
OB: G3P3, three vaginal deliveries, youngest is 14.
FH: mother T2DM and "her bladder dropped" (pelvic organ prolapse). Maternal grandmother hypothyroid. Father had gallstones.
SH: 3rd grade teacher, before that worked retail sales for years. Married, 3 kids. Never smoker. No alcohol at all.
Allergies: NKDA.

ROS: negative except as above. No polyuria/polydipsia. No numbness in feet. No chest pain or SOB.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. BMI ~31. Pleasant, well appearing. Thyroid not enlarged, no nodules. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abd soft, obese, nontender, no organomegaly. Feet: skin intact, monofilament intact both feet, DP pulses 2+. Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix normal, Pap/HPV collected. No visible prolapse.

A/P
- T2DM: continue metformin. A1c, CMP, lipids, urine microalbumin today. Optometry referral list given for dilated exam.
- Hypothyroid: TSH.
- Obesity: talked portion size, walking after school. She'd rather do it on her own for now.
- Constipation: fiber/fluids, she's comfortable with her routine.
- HM: Pap/HPV today. Tdap today (no record of one). HCV and HIV screens. Mammogram ordered. Colon screening at 45 - discussed, she'd like to wait until next year.
- Records requested from prior office.
Return ~6 months, sooner prn. She has my cell.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outpatient Gastroenterology Consultation
Date of service: 12/21/2022
Referring: Primary care

Reason: postprandial right upper quadrant discomfort with bloating.

Ms. Pomeroy is a 47-year-old teacher with type 2 diabetes, obesity, hypothyroidism and longstanding constipation. For several weeks she has had episodes of right upper abdominal discomfort after eating, with a bloated feeling, usually after larger or fattier evening meals. She has had no fever, no vomiting and no jaundice.

PMH: T2DM, obesity, hypothyroidism, chronic constipation. PSH: none abdominal or pelvic.
Medications: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, multivitamin, ibuprofen as needed.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family: father with gallstones; mother diabetes and pelvic organ prolapse; grandmother hypothyroid.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol. She has been trying to lose weight with diet changes.

Exam: comfortable. Anicteric. Abdomen soft, nontender today, no hepatosplenomegaly. Exam otherwise unremarkable.

Data: AST 28, ALT 25, alkaline phosphatase 79, total bilirubin 0.7. Ultrasound today shows multiple small radiolucent-appearing gallstones without wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid; duct not dilated.

Impression: symptomatic cholelithiasis, mild, without complication.

Plan: We discussed laparoscopic cholecystectomy as the definitive treatment. She does not want surgery at this time. Given small stones and a functioning gallbladder, she will try oral dissolution with ursodiol 250 mg three times daily with meals, understanding that it is slow, may not work, and stones can recur. Low-fat diet; avoid rapid weight loss. Repeat ultrasound in about 12 months. She knows to seek care for fever, persistent pain, vomiting or yellowing.

Gastroenterology

Orthopedics & Sports Medicine
Visit: 03/21/2023

Thank you for sending Ms. Pomeroy, 47, with type 2 diabetes, obesity and hypothyroidism, for right plantar foot pain of about three months that has been getting worse. Her pain is most intense with her first morning steps and when she stands after sitting. She teaches and stands for most of the school day, which aggravates it.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, multivitamin, ibuprofen as needed.
Allergies: NKDA. Social: never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: tenderness to palpation along the anterior plantar calcaneus. Pain reproduced with passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass). No swelling. Neurovascularly intact.

Imaging: right foot radiographs today demonstrate a small calcaneal spur, no fracture.

Assessment: right plantar fasciitis; small calcaneal spur, incidental to symptoms.

Plan: continue daily stretching and supportive footwear; over-the-counter arch support; ice; anti-inflammatory as needed with food. Return in 6 weeks.

documents.title: Gynecology Consultation
documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
Gynecology Consultation, date of visit 12/27/2023

Referred by primary care for urinary incontinence.

Ms. Pomeroy is a 48-year-old with type 2 diabetes (well controlled on metformin), obesity, hypothyroidism and chronic constipation, previously seen elsewhere for gallstones and plantar fasciitis. For six months she has leaked urine both with coughing or sneezing and with abrupt, intense urgency that she is not always able to suppress, with several accidents on the way to the toilet. She denies blood in the urine, painful urination and nighttime voiding. Her bladder diary shows voiding about every 90 minutes during the school day with 3 urge episodes per week.

OB history: G3P3, three vaginal births. Surgical history: none abdominal or pelvic.
Medications: metformin, levothyroxine, multivitamin, ibuprofen as needed. Allergies: none known.
Family history: mother with pelvic organ prolapse and diabetes.
Social: teacher; no tobacco or alcohol.

Exam: BMI 31. Abdomen without suprapubic tenderness or mass. Cough stress test with a comfortably full bladder provokes a small amount of leakage. Pelvic exam: normal external genitalia, no significant anterior or apical descent. Neurologic exam of the lower extremities and perineal sensation normal.

Urinalysis: no evidence of infection, no blood.

Assessment: urge urinary incontinence (overactive bladder), urge-predominant, with a minor stress component.

Plan: first-line behavioral therapy - timed voiding with gradual lengthening of intervals, urge suppression techniques, reduce caffeine and diet soda, avoid constipation. Referral to pelvic floor physical therapy. Revisit in 3-4 months; we can consider medication if behavioral treatment is not enough.

Thank you for this referral.

Reason for referral: bulge at the anus with defecation.

Ms. Pomeroy is 49, with chronic constipation and prior care for urinary incontinence earlier this year. For about six months she has felt a bulge in the perineum, most obvious while she moves her bowels. At times it protrudes through the anal canal, particularly after prolonged standing or coughing.

PMH: type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity, chronic constipation, overactive bladder, gallstones (asymptomatic). PSH: no abdominal or pelvic surgery. OB: three vaginal deliveries.
Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, multivitamin, ibuprofen as needed. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: mother with pelvic organ prolapse. SH: teacher, never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: abdomen soft, nontender, unremarkable. With straining, a soft, red, circumferential doughnut-shaped protrusion appears at the anal verge and goes back on its own when she lies flat. Digital rectal exam confirms a full-thickness rectal prolapse.

Assessment: full-thickness rectal prolapse in the setting of chronic straining and multiparity.

Plan: start daily polyethylene glycol 3350 17 g plus a fiber goal of 25-30 g per day to soften stools and stop straining. Discussed that surgical repair is the definitive treatment; she would like to try bowel management first. Return in 6 weeks, sooner if it will not reduce.

documents.title: Surgeon visit
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The surgeon said it is a rectal prolapse. I'm taking the powder every day. Do I need to stop it before I start school again?

documents.title: RE: Surgeon visit

documents.body: Read the surgeon's letter. No, keep the polyethylene glycol going every day, it's safe long term. Adjust to half a capful if stools get too loose. Added it to your med list.

documents.body: Diabetic eye exam 07/22/2024. Dilated both eyes. Optic nerves healthy, maculae flat and dry, no hemorrhages, microaneurysms or exudates. No diabetic retinopathy. Return in 12 months.

documents.title: General Surgery Follow-up
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
General Surgery follow-up, 08/19/2024

Ms. Pomeroy, 49, returns because things are worse since July despite daily polyethylene glycol. She still describes the perianal bulge, which has been present about six months in all and is most noticeable with bowel movements. It sometimes goes back on its own, but now she often has to push it back in by hand. She notices occasional mucus discharge and, recently, some fecal incontinence.

No interval surgery. Medications: metformin, levothyroxine, polyethylene glycol, multivitamin, ibuprofen as needed. NKDA.

Exam: on straining, a reddish doughnut-shaped mass with concentric mucosal rings protrudes from the anus and reduces when she stops. Decreased anal sphincter tone on digital exam.

Assessment: full-thickness rectal prolapse, progressive, now with mucus discharge and fecal incontinence.

Plan: recommend laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy. Risks including mesh complications, recurrence, bleeding, infection and change in bowel function were reviewed; she wishes to proceed. Colonoscopy beforehand. Preoperative medical evaluation by primary care. Tentative surgery date late October.

documents.title: Pre-op
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Surgeon's office requesting pre-op H&P within 30 days of 10/22 surgery. Booked 9/26 after school. Colonoscopy 9/17 already set by GI.

documents.title: Colonoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Colonoscopy, 09/17/2024
Indication: evaluation of the colon before planned rectopexy for rectal prolapse; average-risk colorectal screening, age 49.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care.
Prep: split-dose, excellent quality.
Findings: the scope was passed to the cecum, identified by the appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve; terminal ileum briefly intubated and normal. Colonic mucosa normal throughout. No polyps, masses or diverticula. Rectum normal on retroflexion. Withdrawal time 9 minutes.
Impression: normal colonoscopy.
Recommendation: proceed with planned surgery; next screening colonoscopy in 10 years.
Allergies: NKDA.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 74. PR 152 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 418 ms. Normal axis. No ST or T wave abnormality.

documents.title: Preoperative Evaluation
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pre-op H&P for laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy 10/22/24 (general surgery).
Prolapse now needs manual reduction at times, mucus, some fecal leakage - this is why she agreed to surgery. Colonoscopy 9/17 normal.
Functional capacity: walks 30+ min, climbs 2 flights of stairs at school carrying supplies, no chest pain or dyspnea. No prior anesthesia except colonoscopy sedation, did fine. No bleeding history. No personal or family anesthesia problems.
Meds: metformin 1000 BID, levothyroxine 100, polyethylene glycol 17 g daily, MVI, ibuprofen prn. NKDA.
PMH: DM2, hypothyroid, obesity, chronic constipation, OAB, gallstones (asymptomatic, declined chole).
Exam: BP/HR per vitals. Airway: Mallampati II. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, NT. No leg swelling.
ECG: normal sinus rhythm.
Labs pending today (CMP, CBC, A1c, TSH; also due UACR/lipids so added).
Assessment: low risk patient for an intermediate-risk procedure. RCRI 0. Acceptable to proceed pending labs.
Peri-op: hold metformin the morning of surgery and resume when eating; take levothyroxine as usual. Stop ibuprofen 7 days prior; acetaminophen ok. Stop multivitamin day before. Will fax to surgeon once labs result.

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Operative Report
Date of surgery: 10/22/2024
Preoperative and postoperative diagnosis: full-thickness rectal prolapse.
Procedure: laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy.
Anesthesia: general endotracheal.
Findings: deep pouch of Douglas; mobile rectum. No other intra-abdominal abnormality; gallbladder not examined in detail.
Description: five-port laparoscopy. Peritoneum incised over the right side of the sacral promontory and carried down along the right side of the rectum into the rectovaginal septum, which was opened toward the pelvic floor. Biologic mesh strip sutured to the anterior rectum and fixed to the sacral promontory with tacks. Peritoneum closed over the mesh. Estimated blood loss 20 mL. No complications. Sponge and needle counts correct.
Disposition: to recovery, stable.

documents.title: Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Discharge Summary
Admitted 10/22/2024, discharged 10/23/2024.
Procedure: laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy for full-thickness rectal prolapse, uncomplicated.
Course: tolerated a regular diet on the evening of surgery; pain controlled with acetaminophen. Voided spontaneously. Glucose 120s-170s while on clears, metformin resumed at dinner on POD 0.
Discharge medications: resume home metformin, levothyroxine, multivitamin; continue polyethylene glycol 3350 17 g daily - do not strain; acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed. Avoid ibuprofen for 1 week.
Activity: no lifting over 10 pounds for 4 weeks.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Follow up: clinic in 6 weeks.

documents.title: Post-op check-in
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called to check in, 2 wks out. Back at school this week on light duty (no recess). Small incisions healing, no fever. Soft BM daily on polyethylene glycol, no bulge. A little gas-pain the first week, gone. Sugars fine, eating normally. Surgeon f/u in December.

documents.title: Postoperative Visit
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
General Surgery postoperative visit, 12/10/2024, seven weeks after laparoscopic ventral mesh rectopexy.
She is doing well. No bulge since surgery. Daily soft bowel movement on polyethylene glycol without straining. Fecal leakage much less frequent - one minor episode of soiling in the past month. Mucus discharge gone. Port sites healed.
Exam: abdomen soft, wounds healed. No prolapse on straining.
Assessment: successful repair of full-thickness rectal prolapse.
Plan: continue polyethylene glycol and fiber long term; avoid straining. Lifting restrictions lifted. Follow up as needed.

Annual exam, 50F.
Year in review: rectopexy Oct 2024, no recurrence. Colonoscopy normal 9/2024 (next 2034). Bladder mostly controlled. Shingrix complete. Eye exam July, no retinopathy.
No RUQ pain since 2023; gallstones still in place, she's aware.

Exam: NAD. Thyroid normal. Heart RRR, no murmurs. Lungs clear. Abd soft, healed port scars, NT, no organomegaly. Breasts without masses. Pelvic: normal external, cervix normal, Pap/HPV collected. Feet intact sensation and pulses.

documents.title: Text with patient
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Texted a photo - eyes look yellow. Says she's been itchy for about two months (thought it was dry winter skin), stools pale, urine dark like tea, and a full feeling under the right ribs. Not really painful. No fever. With her known gallstones this needs labs and imaging today, not something I can get done quickly enough in the office during school break. Advised ED in the morning, sooner if fever, pain or vomiting. She'll go first thing.

events.reason: Itching, pale stools, dark urine, RUQ fullness

reports.text: Liver measures 18.5 cm in craniocaudal length, mildly enlarged, with normal echotexture and no focal lesion. Mild intrahepatic biliary prominence. Common bile duct dilated to 9 mm; distal duct obscured by bowel gas. Gallbladder contains multiple shadowing stones; wall normal thickness; no pericholecystic fluid; no sonographic tenderness. Pancreatic head poorly seen. Right kidney normal.
reports.conclusion: Cholelithiasis with dilated common bile duct, suggesting distal obstruction; MRCP recommended. Mild hepatomegaly.

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency Department Physician Record
Date of visit: 12/23/2025
Sent by her primary physician.

HPI: 50-year-old woman with gallstones known since 2022 (failed ursodiol, declined surgery) and type 2 diabetes, here with two months of generalized itching, light-colored stools and dark urine, plus a sense of fullness in the right upper abdomen. She denies significant pain, fever, rigors or vomiting.

PMH: type 2 diabetes, obesity, hypothyroidism, chronic constipation, overactive bladder, rectal prolapse repaired 2024. PSH: laparoscopic rectopexy 2024.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, polyethylene glycol daily, multivitamin, ibuprofen PRN.
Allergies: NKDA. Social: no alcohol, never smoker.

Exam: afebrile, vitals stable. Icteric skin and sclerae. Abdomen soft and nontender without masses; liver edge palpable, mildly enlarged.

Labs: total bilirubin 2.8, direct 1.9, alkaline phosphatase 420, AST 50, ALT 55. CBC, lipase, BMP and INR unremarkable.
Ultrasound: gallstones; CBD 9 mm; liver mildly enlarged.

MDM: cholestatic jaundice with dilated duct in a patient with gallstones, most likely choledocholithiasis; no signs of cholangitis. Malignant obstruction less likely but needs exclusion with MRCP.

Disposition: admitted to the hospitalist service with GI and surgery consultation.

documents.title: ERCP Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography
Date: 12/24/2025
Indication: obstructive jaundice; MRCP with distal common bile duct stone.
Sedation: general anesthesia.
Findings: normal major papilla. Deep biliary cannulation achieved. Cholangiogram: CBD dilated to about 10 mm with a 7 mm filling defect in the distal duct and smaller debris above it. Biliary sphincterotomy performed. Duct swept with an extraction balloon, removing one 7 mm stone and several fragments and sludge. Final occlusion cholangiogram showed no residual filling defects and good drainage. Pancreatic duct not injected.
Impression: choledocholithiasis, cleared.
Recommendation: cholecystectomy this admission; trend liver tests.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
Hospital Discharge Summary
Admission 12/23/2025 - Discharge 12/27/2025

Principal diagnosis: obstructive jaundice due to choledocholithiasis.
Secondary: symptomatic cholelithiasis; type 2 diabetes; hypothyroidism.

Course:
Admitted from the ED with two months of pruritus, pale stools, dark urine and RUQ fullness, icteric with mild hepatomegaly. Bilirubin 2.8 (direct 1.9), alkaline phosphatase 420, AST 50, ALT 55. Ultrasound showed gallstones and a 9 mm CBD.
12/24: MRCP - 7 mm stone in the distal common bile duct, mild intrahepatic ductal dilation, multiple gallbladder stones, normal pancreas with no mass. ERCP the same afternoon with sphincterotomy and balloon clearance of the duct.
12/26: laparoscopic cholecystectomy by general surgery, uncomplicated. Previous rectopexy mesh noted in the pelvis, not disturbed. Bilirubin 1.6, alkaline phosphatase 310 that morning.
12/27: bilirubin 1.3, alkaline phosphatase 265, AST 34, ALT 41. Itching resolved, tolerating diet, pain controlled with acetaminophen.
Diabetes: metformin held around procedures, glucose 140-190 on a carbohydrate-controlled diet; metformin resumed 12/26 evening.
No antibiotics required (no cholangitis).

Discharge medications: metformin 1000 mg twice daily; levothyroxine 100 mcg daily; polyethylene glycol 3350 17 g daily; multivitamin daily; acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed for incisional pain. Avoid ibuprofen for one week.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Pathology: gallbladder with cholesterol stones, no dysplasia or malignancy.
Follow-up: primary care within 1-2 weeks with hepatic panel; general surgery in 4-6 weeks.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: TCM call 2 days after discharge. Pt home, eating, mild soreness at incisions, acetaminophen twice a day. Itching gone, urine lighter. Meds reconciled with discharge summary. Appt 1/6 confirmed.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospital f/u. Admitted 12/23-12/27: obstructive jaundice from CBD stone, ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone clearance 12/24, lap chole 12/26. Path benign. Discharge summary and ERCP report reviewed.
Now: feels like herself. No itch, color back, stools brown, urine normal. Incisions sore only when she twists. Back to school next week. Using acetaminophen once a day, stopping soon. No fever.
Meds reconciled: metformin, levothyroxine, PEG, MVI; acetaminophen prn. Ibuprofen ok again now.
Exam: sclerae anicteric. Abd soft, laparoscopic incisions clean, mild tenderness at umbilical port. No hepatomegaly on my exam today.
A/P:
- Choledocholithiasis/cholelithiasis s/p ERCP and cholecystectomy: hepatic panel today. Jaundice resolved clinically.
- DM2: glucose ran a bit high inpatient, A1c due at March visit.
Surgery post-op visit early Feb.
